title: (No AI) Musicians-turned-detectives are hunting for AI grifters
author: Charles Pulliam-Moore
content:
![A digital illustration depicting Nihil Young and Max “H4RRIS” Harris.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268714_finding_and_shaming_AI_grifters_CVirginia.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0,0,85.33125,89.314310632479)

As [audio-focused generative tools](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/979345/suno-studio-2-0-midi-chatbot-custom-effects) and platforms have [gotten more sophisticated](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/976636/suno-will-start-scanning-outputs-for-copyright-infringment), the internet has become increasingly filled with [AI-generated music](https://www.billboard.com/music/rb-hip-hop/tyga-admits-ai-starface-album-1236311004/) whose melodies and vocals are algorithmically derived from the work of human artists. While some of the people pumping out this kind of content [immediately own up to using AI](https://www.npr.org/2025/06/17/nx-s1-5431544/timbaland-ai-music-suno-stage-zero-tata-generative), others have [denied using the technology](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/976801/fenix-flexin-rubberz-ai-song-treblo) until increasing public scrutiny [forced them to tell the truth](https://ca.rollingstone.com/music/fenix-flexin-admits-use-ai-rubberz/).

For musicians - especially those creating art in technologically-focused spaces like electronic dance music - the increasingly complicated question of what is "real" and what isn't feels particularly urgent and personal …

[Read the full story at The Verge.](https://www.theverge.com/entertainment/985866/h4rris-nihil-young-edm-suno-ai)

title: (No AI) Trump’s EPA wants to let data centers hide their air pollution
author: Justine Calma
content:
![Graphic image of a data center.](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/06/STKS528_DATA_CENTERS2_C.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0,0,100,100)

Just as new data centers [face growing backlash](https://www.theverge.com/science/841169/ai-data-center-opposition) from neighboring communities, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is about to make it harder for people to weigh in on any pollution those centers create.

The EPA plans to toss out a federal rule requiring public notice and an opportunity to comment when certain industrial sites apply for an air permit. Advocates warn that the move would allow data center developers and other industries to break ground without giving nearby residents a say, or even a warning that construction is planned.

"You can see why that would be so interesting to an administration that wants to rush through the …
